tagline: A pastor's letter to shaken churches after a painful split, teaching them how to know God, how to know the truth about Jesus, and how to know they belong.
overview:
First John reads less like a letter than like a sermon written down. It has no greeting, no named sender, no named readers, and no farewell. What it has is a pastor's urgent voice speaking to people he calls “little children”, churches that have just been through a split. A group that once worshiped with them has walked out (2:19), taking with it a new teaching about Jesus and leaving the people who stayed unsettled. Were the ones who left more spiritual? Had the ones who stayed missed something? Could they be sure they knew God at all?

John answers by circling back, again and again, to three tests. The first is belief: the one who knows God confesses that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, come in the flesh. The second is obedience: the one who knows God keeps his commandments and walks as Jesus walked. The third is love: the one who knows God loves his brothers and sisters, not in words only but with open hands. Along the way the letter says some of the most famous things in the Bible about God: that God is light (1:5), that God is love (4:8, 4:16), and that love is seen in this, that God sent his Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins (4:10).

The letter matters because the questions it answers never went away. People still ask whether Jesus was really human or only seemed to be, whether belief matters if one is kind, and whether a person who struggles with sin can have any confidence before God. John refuses to let belief, obedience, and love be pulled apart. He writes, he says, so that his readers may know that they have eternal life (5:13).
author:
The letter never names its author. The writer speaks as an eyewitness, one of a group who heard, saw, and touched the Word of life (1:1-3), and he writes with the authority of a senior leader over churches he treats as his children. From the second century on, the church attributed the letter to John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, the same John traditionally credited with the Fourth Gospel. Irenaeus, writing about AD 180, quotes it as John's. The language and ideas are strikingly close to John's Gospel: light and darkness, truth and lies, abiding, being born of God, the world, love, the new commandment. Most scholars agree that the Gospel and the letters come from the same circle, and many think the same hand wrote both.

There is a real debate about which John. Eusebius, the fourth-century church historian, quotes the early second-century bishop Papias as naming both the apostle John and a John he calls the elder, and some scholars think the elder was a different person who led the churches of Asia late in the first century. Second and Third John open with the words “The elder”. Others hold that the elder and the apostle were the same man, using a title that fit an aged leader. Still others speak of a Johannine community, a network of churches and teachers shaped by the beloved disciple, from which these writings came. The letter's own claim is that its author stood close to the events of Jesus' life.
date: The letter gives no date. Most scholars place it late in the first century, somewhere around AD 85 to 100, after John's Gospel had been written or while its traditions were well established, since the letter seems to assume that way of speaking about Jesus. A minority dates it earlier, in the 60s, before the fall of Jerusalem. The order of the three letters is not certain either, though First John is usually thought to have been written first or alongside the other two.
setting:
Early Christian tradition places John's last years in Ephesus, the great port city of the Roman province of Asia (the western part of modern Turkey), and most readers assume the letter was written for churches in that region. These were house churches, meeting in homes, scattered through a Greek-speaking world full of temples, trade guilds, philosophies, and religious movements.

The immediate setting is a schism. Some who had belonged to the fellowship left (2:19), and John calls them liars and antichrists because they deny that Jesus is the Christ (2:22) and refuse to confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh (4:2-3). The exact shape of their teaching is debated. Many scholars see an early form of docetism, from the Greek word dokeo, to seem, the belief that the divine Christ only seemed to have a real human body, because a spiritual being could not truly be joined to flesh or die. Irenaeus reports that a teacher named Cerinthus, active in Asia in John's time, taught that the divine Christ came upon the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the crucifixion. Whether John is answering Cerinthus himself, a related group, or something less developed, the pressure is clear: a spirituality that despised the body, claimed special knowledge, and treated sin and love of neighbor as unimportant.
purpose: John writes to reassure and to steady. He wants the believers who stayed to know that they are not second-class, that they have the anointing of the Spirit and know the truth (2:20-21), and that they have eternal life (5:13). He also wants to give them clear tests for telling true teaching from false: what a person confesses about Jesus, whether he keeps God's commands, and whether he loves his brothers and sisters. The letter is pastoral first and polemical second. Its warnings about the false teachers serve its main aim, which is that the readers may have fellowship with the Father and the Son, and joy that is complete (1:3-4).
story: First John comes near the end of the New Testament story, in the second or third generation of the church, when the apostles were dying and questions about who Jesus was had begun to divide communities from within. It stands beside John's Gospel as its companion. The Gospel was written so that readers might believe that Jesus is the Christ and have life in his name (John 20:31); the letter is written to people who already believe, so that they may know they have that life (5:13). Behind it lies the whole Old Testament hope of a God who would dwell with his people, write his law on their hearts, and give them a new heart. Ahead of it, Revelation, which tradition connects with the same churches of Asia, shows the same Christ addressing those churches in their trials.
christ: First John is fiercely concerned with who Jesus is. He is the Word of life whom the apostles heard, saw, and touched (1:1), the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed (1:2). He is the Christ, the Son of God, who came in the flesh, and the letter treats denial of this as the mark of antichrist. He is the Righteous One who speaks to the Father on behalf of sinners (2:1), the atoning sacrifice for our sins and for the whole world (2:2, 4:10), the one who appeared to take away sins and destroy the works of the devil (3:5, 3:8), and the one who came by water and blood (5:6). The letter ends by calling him “the true God and eternal life” (5:20), one of the New Testament's clearest statements of Christ's deity, though grammarians debate whether that phrase refers to the Son or to the Father. Christ is also the pattern: his laying down of his life defines what love is (3:16).
reading:
Don't expect a straight line of argument. John works like a composer with a few themes, returning to light, love, truth, obedience, and belief, each time from a slightly different angle. Read it slowly and listen for the repetitions. His language is simple and his sentences short, but the simplicity is deceptive.

Two misreadings are common. The first takes the letter's absolute statements, such as that the one born of God does not keep on sinning (3:9), as a demand for sinless perfection, which contradicts John's own words that anyone who says he has no sin deceives himself (1:8). The second reads the tests of the letter as a checklist to make believers anxious, when John's stated purpose is assurance. Remember too that the letter addresses a real schism. Its sharp language about liars and antichrists is aimed at specific teachers who had denied Christ's coming in the flesh, not at every person who struggles or doubts.

structure.title: Prologue: the Word of life
structure.summary: The author and his fellow witnesses proclaim what they heard, saw, and touched, so that readers may share their fellowship with the Father and the Son.

structure.title: Walking in the light
structure.summary: God is light. Walking with him means confessing sin, keeping his commands, loving one's brother, refusing to love the world, and holding to the truth about the Son against the antichrists who have left.

structure.title: Children of God
structure.summary: Those whom the Father has loved and called his children practice righteousness and love one another, as Jesus laid down his life for us.

structure.title: Testing the spirits; God is love
structure.summary: True spirits confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh. God is love, shown in the sending of his Son, and those who know him love one another without fear.

structure.title: Faith, testimony, and assurance
structure.summary: Faith in the Son overcomes the world. God's testimony about his Son gives life, and believers can know they have eternal life, pray with confidence, and keep themselves from idols.

themes.title: Fellowship with God
themes.body: The letter opens with the aim of fellowship (koinonia), a shared life with the Father, the Son, and one another (1:3). John speaks of it in several ways: knowing God, abiding or remaining in him, being born of him, being his children. This is not a mood but a relationship, and it has visible marks in belief, obedience, and love.

themes.title: The Word made flesh
themes.body: Against teachers who denied that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, John insists on the physical reality of the incarnation: the life of God was heard, seen, and touched. The cross was a real death in real blood. A Christ who only seemed to be human could not be the atoning sacrifice for sins, and a spirituality that despises the body will soon despise the neighbor.

themes.title: Love as the family likeness
themes.body: God is love, and his love was shown in sending his Son. Those born of God bear the family resemblance. John makes the test concrete: love is laying down one's life and opening one's hand to a brother in need (3:16-18). No one can claim to love the unseen God while hating the brother he can see (4:20).

themes.title: Sin, forgiveness, and holiness
themes.body: John holds together two truths that are easily pulled apart. Believers still sin, and those who deny it deceive themselves, but the blood of Jesus cleanses and God forgives those who confess (1:7-9). At the same time, the one born of God does not settle into a life of sin, because Christ came to take sin away. Grace is neither excuse nor impossible demand.

themes.title: Assurance
themes.body: The letter's closing purpose statement is that believers may know they have eternal life (5:13). Its tests are meant to steady people who had been told they lacked something. Confidence before God rests on his testimony about his Son and on the Spirit he has given, and even when our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts (3:20).

keyChapters.why: The prologue's eyewitness claim, and the teaching that God is light and that those who confess their sins are forgiven and cleansed.
Christ as advocate and atoning sacrifice, the old and new commandment, and the departure of the antichrists.
The Father's love in calling us his children, and love defined by Jesus laying down his life.
Testing the spirits, and the great statement that God is love, shown in the sending of his Son.
Faith that overcomes the world, God's testimony about his Son, and the letter's purpose of assurance.
